Financial planning · Fees, inflation and long-term investing · Visual planning guide

A 2% fee is a third of a 6% return, but more than half of what beats inflation: measure fund fees against the real return

A fund fee is quoted against the whole return, but what builds purchasing power is the return left after inflation. See how the same fee takes a much larger share of that real return, what it does to a monthly saving plan in today’s dollars, and how Canadian inflation has actually varied since 1996.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Measure a fund fee against the return left after inflation, not the return before it

The plan starts with $10,000 and adds $500 a month, raised with inflation each year for 25 years. In today’s dollars it ends at $236,225 with the 0.5% fee and $189,635 with the 2% fee; you put in the equivalent of $158,011. Returns are smooth and hypothetical, before tax, and not a forecast of any fund.

The central idea

A fee is a percentage of everything you hold, charged every year whether the fund rises, falls or merely keeps up with prices. Measured against the return before inflation it can look modest. Measured against the part of the return that actually increases what your money can buy, it is often the largest single cost in the plan. With a 6% return before fees and 2.5% inflation, a 2% fee takes about 35% of the return but about 61% of the real return; a 0.5% fee takes about 15% of it. The fee is known in advance while returns and inflation are not, so it is worth comparing in the same real terms as the goal it is meant to fund.

01

Two ways to describe the same fee

Suppose a balanced fund earns 6% a year before its fee and charges 2% of assets. Taken in the usual way, the fee is about a third of the return: the fund reports roughly 3.9% instead of 6%. That framing understates what the fee costs a long-term saver, because 6% is not what your money gains in buying power. If prices rise 2.5% a year, most of the return only keeps your savings where they were.

This guide measures the fee against the real return, the growth left after inflation. That is the part that pays for a larger retirement, a home or an education, and it is where the fee takes its largest bite. The calculator lets you set the return, inflation and two fees to compare, and follows a saving plan in today’s dollars.

02

Where the return goes

The fee is a percentage of the balance, taken from the grown fund each year. So a 6% return with a 2% fee grows the fund by 1.06 × 0.98, or 3.88% a year; the fee takes 2.12 percentage points, slightly more than 2 because it is charged on the year’s growth too. Inflation then divides that by 1.025, leaving a real return of about 1.35%. The second chart shows these three steps as a waterfall: 6% before fees, minus 2.12 points of fee, minus about 2.53 points of lost purchasing power, leaves 1.35%. The inflation step is a little above 2.5 points because inflation erodes the fund’s growth as well as its starting value.

Without any fee, the same 6% would have been a real return of about 3.41%. The fee therefore removes about 61% of the real return, against about 35% of the return before inflation. With a 0.5% fee the real return is about 2.90%, and the fee takes about 15% of the real return instead of about 9% of the nominal one. The difference between the two descriptions grows as inflation rises: the fee stays a fixed percentage of assets, while the real return it is taken from shrinks.

03

How much inflation has Canada actually had?

The first chart uses Statistics Canada’s all-items CPI. Measured from one year’s average prices to the next, inflation was between 0.3% (2009) and 6.8% (2022) from 1996 to 2025, and averaged about 2.64% a year over the ten years to 2025 and about 2.17% over the twenty years to 2025. In September 2026 the index stood at 170.0, 3.1% above September 2025. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range.

Those are dated observations, not a forecast. The ten-year average line shows how a few years can move a long average: it rose after 2021 because of the surge in 2022 and 2023. For planning, test a range. The guide to inflation expectations shows what households and businesses expect, and the personal inflation guide explains why your own costs may rise faster or slower than the CPI.

04

What the difference does to a saving plan

The third chart follows a plan that starts with CAD 10,000 already invested and adds CAD 500 from each month’s pay, raised with inflation each year so the effort stays the same in real terms. After 25 years, the contributions are worth about CAD 158,011 in today’s dollars. With no fee at all, a reference line rather than an available product, the plan would be worth about CAD 254,712 of today’s money, a real gain of about CAD 96,700. With a 0.5% fee it is worth about CAD 236,225, keeping about four-fifths of that gain. With a 2% fee it is worth about CAD 189,635, keeping about a third.

The fees themselves, deducted month by month and converted to today’s dollars, come to about CAD 13,745 at 0.5% and CAD 47,840 at 2%. The gap between the two plans, about CAD 46,589, is larger than the difference in fees because every dollar deducted would otherwise have kept growing.

The same arithmetic applies to money you already have. A CAD 100,000 lump sum invested for 25 years with the same assumptions would be worth about CAD 204,234 in today’s dollars at 0.5% and about CAD 139,702 at 2%. Whether to invest a lump sum at once or in stages is a separate decision about market timing, covered in the phased-investing guide; the fee applies either way once the money is in the fund.

05

When inflation is high, the same fee can erase the real return

The heatmap keeps the 6% return before fees and changes inflation and the fee. With 1% inflation, a 2% fee still leaves a real return of about 2.85%. With 4% inflation the same fee leaves about −0.12%, and with 5% about −1.07%: the fund still reports a positive return of 3.88%, but it loses purchasing power after its fee. A 0.5% fee at 4% inflation leaves about 1.41%.

This matters most for the parts of a plan with low expected returns. A balanced fund’s bond holdings, or a conservative fund, may expect a return before fees not far above inflation, so a fee of 1.5% to 2% can absorb most or all of the real return of that portion. The guide to stocks and bonds falling together shows how inflation can also hurt both parts of a balanced fund at once. None of this says a higher fee is never worth paying. It says the fee should be judged against the service it buys and the real return you can reasonably expect, not against the headline return.

06

Fees, tax and the account: three separate layers

The fee is paid inside the fund in every account. Tax depends on the account, not on the fund:

  • TFSA. CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. A fee still reduces the return, and with no tax to share the cost, its whole effect falls on you.
  • RRSP. CRA says income earned in the plan is usually exempt from tax while it remains there, and payments from it are generally taxed. The fee reduces the balance that is later taxed on withdrawal.
  • Non-registered account. A fund’s management expense ratio (MER) is paid out of the fund’s assets, so it reduces the income and gains the fund distributes or accumulates; it is not a separate deduction on your return. CRA allows certain fees for managing or advising on non-registered investments to be claimed as carrying charges on line 22100, but not fees for registered plans such as RRSPs and TFSAs. Tax is charged on nominal gains and income, not real ones, so after tax the real return is lower still; the guide to tax on inflation gains shows how much.

A fund is not tax-free in itself. The same fund units held in a TFSA, an RRSP or a taxable account are taxed differently, and the fee comes off the return in all three.

07

Practical checks

  • Read the MER in the Fund Facts and translate it. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site says MERs run from under 1% to over 3%, that they are charged whether or not the fund does well, and that reported returns are already after them. Divide the fee by the real return you expect, not by the headline return.
  • Know what a trailing commission pays for. In advice-sold series the MER includes a trailing commission to the dealer; the series comparison guide sets the advice-included and fee-based routes side by side.
  • Compare like with like. A cheaper fund with a different mix of stocks and bonds has different risk. Changing the fee is not the same as changing the investment, as the long-term fee guide explains.
  • Raise contributions with prices. With the monthly saving left flat, the default plan with the 2% fee ends at about CAD 148,935 in today’s dollars against contributions worth CAD 121,807. The guide to indexing contributions shows the difference indexing makes.
  • Keep the comparison in real terms throughout. Set your goal in today’s dollars, use a real return after fees and tax, and the plan is consistent. Mixing a nominal return with a goal in today’s prices overstates what the plan will buy; see the inflation and purchasing power guide.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Returns and inflation are constant every year. Real funds rise and fall, sometimes sharply, and the order of good and bad years matters for a saving plan; a recovery from any fall by a particular date is not assured.
  • The fee is a single percentage of assets. Real costs can include trading costs inside the fund, sales charges, account fees and separate advice fees with sales tax, which may not appear in the MER.
  • No tax is calculated. Savings and fees are converted to today’s dollars using one inflation rate, which may differ from your own costs.
  • The return before fees is an assumption, not an estimate for any fund. A higher-fee fund might earn more or less before fees than a lower-fee one; only the fee is known in advance.
  • None of this predicts future returns or inflation, and none of it is a recommendation of any fund or account.
